t: For expenses necessary to enable the United States to meet its obligations under the Convention between the United States and Mexico, signed August 29, 1963, and to carry out the American-Mexican Chamizal Convention Act of 1964, $2,700,000, to remain available until expended: Provided, That this appropriation shall not be available for expenses of operation and maintenance of works provided for in said Convention and Act.

fable.w: This section only appropriates funds to meet obligations under an existing treaty and to carry out the Chamizal Convention Act. The tempting reading is that the reference to a Convention with Mexico signals coordination with an outside party, but that agreement was already concluded and the text sets up no consultation, hearing, comment process, advisory body, or right to sue. No party outside the federal government is brought into any federal decision here.
fable.s: For expenses necessary to enable the United States to meet its obligations under the Convention between the United States and Mexico, signed August 29, 1963

qwen_block.w: This section is a standard appropriations provision that authorizes the expenditure of funds to meet treaty obligations. It does not establish any process for consultation, coordination, or participation with outside parties (such as the public, states, or non-federal entities) in making a federal decision. The mention of the Convention with Mexico refers to the legal basis for the spending, not a participatory mechanism within the statute itself.
qwen_block.s: For expenses necessary to enable the United States to meet its obligations under the Convention between the United States and Mexico, signed August 29, 1963, and to carry out the American-Mexican Chamizal Convention Act of 1964, $2,700,000, to remain available until expended

opus.w: This section is an appropriation that funds obligations under a treaty signed in 1963. It requires no consultation, coordination, hearing or advisory input from anyone outside the federal government before a future decision. Mentioning a past bilateral convention with Mexico is like the past agreement in Example 5: it does not create a new outside-party process.
opus.s: For expenses necessary to enable the United States to meet its obligations under the Convention between the United States and Mexico, signed August 29, 1963, and to carry out the American-Mexican Chamizal Convention Act of 1964, $2,700,000, to remain available until expended
opus.b: The tempting reading is that a convention with Mexico brings a foreign government (an outside party) into a federal decision. That fails because the section only appropriates money to meet obligations under an existing, already-signed treaty. It sets up no consultation, hearing, committee, comment period or right to sue for any future federal decision.

qwen_chat.w: This section is an appropriation clause authorizing funds for the United States to meet its treaty obligations. It does not establish a process for consulting with or coordinating with outside parties (such as the public, states, or even Mexico) in the context of making a federal decision. The mention of the Convention is the basis for the expenditure, not a description of a participatory process.
qwen_chat.s: For expenses necessary to enable the United States to meet its obligations under the Convention between the United States and Mexico, signed August 29, 1963, and to carry out the American-Mexican Chamizal Convention Act of 1964, $2,700,000, to remain available until expended
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that "meeting obligations under the Convention" implies coordination with Mexico, an outside party. However, the text itself is purely an appropriation clause authorizing funds for the U.S. to fulfill its side of a treaty. It does not describe a process of consultation, hearing, or advisory input from non-federal entities into a federal decision-making process. It is a funding authorization, not a participation mechanism.
